newsitem.title: ITALY: Ex-central banker says Italy EMU delay no disaster.
newsitem.headline: Ex-central banker says Italy EMU delay no disaster.

text.p: Joining Europe's single currency six or 12 months after its planned 1999 start would not be a catastrophe for Italy and would be better than going in half-prepared, former central banker Tommaso Padoa Schioppa told a newspaper on Friday.

But the next four months will be crucial for Italy in its bid to clean up the public accounts in time to join economic and monetary union (EMU) at its 1999 start, Padoa Schioppa said in the interview with La Repubblica.
"It's a game we're going to play in the next four months. It's impossible to win without welfare reforms," the former deputy director general of the Bank of Italy said.

Italy is striving to slash its budget deficit to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) by the end of 1997 from around 6.8 percent last year, in order to meet one of the key EMU qualification criteria set out in the Maastricht treaty.
A European Union source in Brussels on Friday said European Commission officials were forecasting a ratio of 3.2 percent.

Italy has taken several budgetary measures in the last few months to hack down the deficit and is in the process of examining the government's latest mini-budget for 15.5 trillion lire of spending cuts and revenue-raising measures.

But critics at home and abroad doubt whether the centre-left government's efforts will have a lasting effect on public finances and say Italy must change its structural spending, particularly its generous pensions system.

Padoa Schioppa, who has just taken over as head of Italy's stock exchange regulator Consob, said it would be "catastrophic" if Italy did not reach the three percent target without having taken structural measures to stabilise the budget deficit.
In that case Italy would arrive at the 1998 appointment when the EU judges who qualifies for EMU entry "in a situation of total uncertainty over the prospects for convergence," he said.
"Not only would we remain on the outside but also without any certainty of a future entry date," he said, adding this would have unforeseeable consequences.

"But the picture would be different if, having consolidated the process of adjustment for 1998 and following years, we found ourselves at the end of 1997 a few fractions of a point above the three percent," he said.
This would either allow Italy immediate entry to EMU or to have a date fixed for entry a little later.
"In any case working to be at the appointment for the established date or at a set date afterwards -- like six or 12 months -- is the essential thing," he said.

He also criticised EU Commissioner Mario Monti for dramatising the distinction between immediate and delayed entry as if the second option were a catastrophe. "(This) seems to me to be excessive, frankly, and politically dangerous."

Monti has been a constant critic of the Italian government's efforts to slash its budget deficit, urging Prime Minister Romano Prodi to bring forward the 1998 budget to show the country's commitment to being an EMU founding member.
